issues.legal_issue: A company director in a fiduciary position cannot unilaterally create a trust or lease over company land in a way that prejudices the company’s rights.
material_facts: The director was entrusted with constructing a building on land owned by the company.
The director offered to complete the building and hand it over to the company as trust property, to be managed by the company’s directors as trustees.

Instead, the director executed a different trust deed naming himself as the first trustee and purporting to make the trust a tenant of the company’s land without the company transferring or agreeing to lease that land.
The company sued for possession of the property.
issues.conclusion: The director could not create a trust over the company’s land or unilaterally create a lease of that land in favour of the trust; his acts could not prejudice the company’s rights.
issues.legal_principle: A director is a trustee of company assets under the director’s control and owes the company fiduciary duties. The Court relied on G. E. Railway v. Turner and Re Forest of Dean, etc., Co. for the principle that directors are trustees of assets under their control. A person cannot create a trust over land belonging to another or unilaterally create a lease in their own favour over that land.

predicates.company_possession_proceeding: A company brought a proceeding seeking possession of its property.
predicates.director_has_fiduciary_control: A director entrusted with company property acted in a fiduciary capacity concerning that property.
predicates.director_unilaterally_creates_interest_o: The director attempted without the company’s agreement to create a trust or lease affecting land owned by the company.

issues.definition: When a company seeks possession and a director acting in a fiduciary capacity unilaterally creates an interest over company land, that interest cannot bind the company.

issues.legal_issue: A licence to construct a building for transfer to a company does not make a different trust arrangement irrevocable, and the licence is deemed revoked when its specific purpose is abandoned or becomes impracticable.
material_facts: The director relied on a licence to construct a building on company land and claimed that expenditure on permanent works made the licence irrevocable.
The licence, if any, was for constructing the building and handing it over to the company as trust property.
The director instead created a different trust arrangement, and the original purpose was abandoned or became impracticable because of his actions.
issues.conclusion: The claimed licence did not protect the different trust arrangement and was not an irrevocable bar to the company’s claim for possession; in any event, a licence for a specific purpose is deemed revoked when that purpose is attained, abandoned, or becomes impracticable.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 60(b) and 62(f) of the Indian Easements Act, 1882, a licence coupled with the execution of a permanent work at the licensee’s expense may be irrevocable, but a licence for a specific purpose is deemed revoked when the purpose is attained, abandoned, or becomes impracticable. The Court referred to Manzoor Ahmad v. Muhammad Abdul Jamil and Dominion of India v. B. B. Sohan Lal, distinguishing them because the terms and purpose of the licence must be examined.

rule.if: civil_possession_proceeding and asserted_licence_for_specific_work and permanent_work_executed_at_own_expense and (different_purpose_pursued or original_purpose_abandoned_or_impracticable)

predicates.civil_possession_proceeding: A party sought possession of property in a civil proceeding.
predicates.asserted_licence_for_specific_work: The person resisting possession relied on permission granted for a particular work and purpose.
predicates.permanent_work_executed_at_own_expense: The person relying on the permission carried out permanent work at their own expense.
predicates.different_purpose_pursued: The person relied on the permission to support an arrangement materially different from the one for which it was granted.
predicates.original_purpose_abandoned_or_impractica: The purpose for which permission was granted was abandoned or became impracticable.

issues.definition: A person who carried out permanent work under permission for a specific purpose cannot use that permission to defeat a possession claim when they pursue a different purpose or the original purpose is abandoned or impracticable.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot rely at the appellate stage on a new defence that was not raised or adjudicated at trial.
material_facts: The director did not plead a licence or its irrevocability in the trial court, and that issue was not adjudicated there.
The director first raised the statutory licence argument in the appeal and relied on it before the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The director could not change the case at the appellate stage by raising a licence defence that had not been pleaded or adjudicated at trial.
issues.legal_principle: A party may not change its case at the appellate stage by introducing a defence that was not raised and adjudicated in the trial court.

rule.if: civil_appeal and defence_not_raised_at_trial and defence_not_adjudicated_at_trial and new_defence_introduced_on_appeal

predicates.civil_appeal: A party pursued an appeal in a civil case.
predicates.defence_not_raised_at_trial: The party did not plead the defence before the trial court.
predicates.defence_not_adjudicated_at_trial: The trial court did not decide the defence.
predicates.new_defence_introduced_on_appeal: The party relied on the previously unraised defence in the appeal.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal, a party cannot introduce a defence that was neither raised nor decided at trial.

issues.legal_issue: A trust arrangement materially different from the one accepted by a company does not provide an equitable defence to the company’s claim for possession.
material_facts: The company accepted an offer under which the building would be completed and handed to the company as trust property, with the company’s directors acting as trustees.
The director executed a materially different trust deed that made the trust a tenant of the company’s land without the company’s agreement.
The director had abandoned reliance on the arrangement set out in the accepted offer, and the amount expended on construction had been returned to him.
issues.conclusion: The different trust deed could not equitably bar the company’s claim for possession, and the director had no equity to enforce as a defence.
issues.legal_principle: Equitable relief cannot be founded on an arrangement materially different from the offer accepted by the company, particularly where the different arrangement purports to burden company land without the company’s agreement. The Court also noted that the director had suffered no loss because his expenditure had been returned.

rule.if: company_possession_proceeding and company_accepted_specific_trust_arrangement and executed_trust_materially_differs and unauthorized_land_tenancy_created and construction_expenditure_returned

predicates.company_possession_proceeding: A company brought a proceeding seeking possession of its property.
predicates.company_accepted_specific_trust_arrangem: The company accepted an offer specifying how property would be held and managed as a trust.
predicates.executed_trust_materially_differs: The trust arrangement actually executed materially departed from the accepted offer.
predicates.unauthorized_land_tenancy_created: The executed arrangement purported to make a trust a tenant of company land without the company’s agreement.
predicates.construction_expenditure_returned: The person who paid for construction had the expenditure returned.

issues.definition: Where a company seeks possession, a materially different trust arrangement that creates an unauthorized tenancy and leaves the person’s construction expenditure returned does not bar possession in equity.
